sources.title: Roberto Burle Marx (Q528922), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-24): English label 'Roberto Burle Marx', description 'Brazilian landscape architect (1909-1994)', instance of human, born 1909-08-04, died 1994-06-04 (a second, conflicting birth month is also recorded), citizen of Brazil; no Korean label and no Korean Wikipedia article. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Roberto Burle Marx' (read in full). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: calls him a Brazilian landscape architect who created many outstanding gardens with important modern buildings and replaced European-style formal gardens with his own country's lush tropical flora; in 1928, studying art in Germany, he became interested in the tropical plants at the Dahlem Botanical Gardens, and after returning in 1930 converted his home into a tropical plant centre; his first garden was for the house of Lucio Costa, then hanging gardens for the Ministry of Education and Health in Rio, and later the Brazilian pavilion at Brussels 1958, the Parque del Este in Caracas, Flamengo Park (1962) and the UNESCO building in Paris; also a painter and a designer of jewelry, fabrics and stage sets, and one of the first prominent Brazilians to criticise the destruction of rainforests. Short reference article, admiring.

William Howard Adams, 'Roberto Burle Marx: The Unnatural Art of the Garden' (The Museum of Modern Art, New York, 1991, exhibition catalogue; read: the introduction, the early-life and Recife chapters, and the passages on his office, Brasilia and Flamengo Park). SUBSTANTIVE, PARTLY CRITICAL SOURCE by an author who watched him work: he developed the habit of sketching in Berlin in 1929, was named head of parks of Pernambuco in 1934 and revitalised Recife's dilapidated squares, searched out indigenous plants 'as a hunter' studying habitats in minute detail, and went on plant-hunting expeditions to the Amazon valley rain forests; his Rio office had an open give-and-take in which everyone joined the first discussions and his partner Haruyoshi Ono worked closely with him; the Parque del Este in Caracas was never completed ('his grand visions respect neither politicians nor budgets'); citing a 1963 Landscape Architecture account, he first declined to take part in Brasilia because the then Belo Horizonte mayor Kubitschek had not paid for earlier work and joined after Kubitschek's 1961 defeat; the author's own critical passage faults Brasilia for disregarding the environment. Admiring of the work but reports friction.

Barbara Boifava, 'Roberto Burle Marx's Cidade Parque', Journal of Landscape Architecture 15(3), 2020, pp. 74-89 (peer-reviewed, read in full from the author PDF; draws on the Burle Marx studio and Sitio archives). SUBSTANTIVE SCHOLARLY SOURCE: from 1949 the Sitio served as an 'ecological experimental laboratory' with systematically gathered Brazilian plants, enlarged by scientific collection expeditions (coletas) with botanists and friends such as the architect Rino Levi; collaboration with the botanists Henrique Lahmeyer de Mello Barreto (Praca Senador Salgado Filho) and Luiz Emygdio de Mello Filho (Flamengo Park) and with his colleagues Tabacow and Ono; Flamengo Park (1961-65) was planned by a working group coordinated by Maria Carlota de Macedo Soares with Affonso Reidy shaping the landfill, and Burle Marx's team designing its eleven sectors; his own statements against deforestation, including a 1983 conference; much of the passion language is his own quoted words.

ICOMOS evaluation of the nomination 'Sitio Roberto Burle Marx (Brazil) No 1620' for the World Heritage List (UNESCO World Heritage Centre advisory evaluation, 2020-21; read). Independent expert evaluation of a Brazilian-prepared nomination: he bought the Santo Antonio da Bica land in 1949 and added land in 1952 and 1960 to house his botanical collection, acquired native tropical plants on special expeditions and acclimatised and tested them there, developed the gardens organically without a previously drawn design, and in 1985 donated the property to the Federal Government, continued to live there and became its first director; ICOMOS also finds the attributes poorly articulated and the design layout less conserved than the plant collections. Institutional evaluation, partly built on the state party's own dossier.

UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Sitio Roberto Burle Marx' (World Heritage List no. 1620, inscribed 2021; description and Outstanding Universal Value read): a 'landscape laboratory' begun in 1949 where over forty years he fused Modernist art and native tropical plants into 'living works of art', 3,500 cultivated species, the first modern tropical garden inscribed on the list. Award-body style institutional text; used for the achievement description only, never for a scored row.

Museu de Arte Moderna do Rio de Janeiro (MAM Rio), project record 'Flamengo Park' (Aterro do Flamengo, 1960-1963; read): lists Maria Carlota Costallat de Macedo Soares as general coordinator and the Burle Marx office, with Roberto Burle Marx as landscape architect and four associated architects, and elsewhere credits his collaborating architects Haruyoshi Ono and Jose Waldemar Tabacow on later works. Short museum record; used for who did what in the team.

Sima Eliovson, 'Biographical notes on Roberto Burle Marx, a unique personality', Journal of the Adelaide Botanic Gardens 1(4), 1979, pp. 263-273 (read in full). Garden writer's profile after visiting him: as a teenager he sold vegetables to import plants, he financed expeditions himself, his Sunday table of friends, his drawings for his office team to translate into plans, his appeals to the press to protect native flora, his worry about the fate of his collection, movable papier-mache sculptures in a courtyard ('change is what makes a garden dynamic'), his home collections of ceramics and flower arrangements. Personal, warm and admiring; not independent of what he told the author.

The Cultural Landscape Foundation, 'Roberto Burle Marx' pioneer profile (read): Berlin 1928 and the Dahlem botanical gardens, experiments with native plants at home after 1930, his first garden for the Schwartz house through Lucio Costa, excursions from his Guaratiba estate to source specimens, the 1955 formalising of his practice as Burle Marx & Cia. Ltda., one of the first Brazilians to speak out against deforestation, teaching at the University of Brazil. Short advocacy-foundation profile.

curiosity.rationale: [src_bm_adams, src_bm_boifava, src_bm_icomos, src_bm_eliovson | 1930s-1960s | exhibition-catalogue biography, scholarly article, expert evaluation, garden-writer profile] Four sources describe plant-hunting expeditions across Brazilian regions and a living collection of about 3,500 species that he then acclimatised and tested; Adams says he searched out indigenous plants 'as a hunter', studying habitats in minute detail, and Eliovson that he financed expeditions himself. The most vivid passages are his own words as quoted by Boifava, so the score is capped; lowered slightly during calibration.

experimentation.rationale: [src_bm_icomos, src_bm_unesco, src_bm_boifava, src_bm_eliovson | 1949-1985 | expert evaluation, award-body text, scholarly article, garden-writer profile] ICOMOS says the Sitio gardens grew organically without a prior plan as plants were tested for use, UNESCO calls it a landscape laboratory and Boifava a bold experimenter with 'artificial ecological associations'; Eliovson reports he would remove movable sculptures and held that change keeps a garden dynamic. The laboratory language across ICOMOS, UNESCO and the Brazilian dossier is one institutional family, so concentration was high; lowered during calibration.

creative_originality.rationale: [src_bm_britannica, src_bm_icomos, src_bm_boifava, src_bm_adams | 1932-1970 | reference biography, expert evaluation, scholarly article, exhibition-catalogue biography] Britannica says he replaced European-style formal gardens with native tropical flora; ICOMOS and Boifava describe the use of abstract-painting aesthetics and a new park-city vocabulary for Rio, and Adams compares the scale of his output to Olmsted's. Support is largely critical and institutional praise of outcomes, and the ICOMOS wording echoes the nomination dossier; lowered during calibration.

aesthetic_sensitivity.rationale: [src_bm_eliovson, src_bm_adams, src_bm_icomos | 1960s-1979 | garden-writer profile, exhibition-catalogue biography, expert evaluation] Eliovson describes a home arranged with ceramics and flower compositions and plants chosen to convey mood; Adams quotes him likening a plant to a brushstroke or a stitch of embroidery; ICOMOS lists dramatic colour contrasts and sinuous forms as design hallmarks. Much of this is description of an artist's output rather than separate behavioural tests, so the row is moderate; lowered during calibration.

cross_domain_range.rationale: [src_bm_britannica, src_bm_boifava, src_bm_adams, src_bm_tclf | 1930-1990 | reference biography, scholarly article, exhibition-catalogue biography, foundation profile] Four sources independently list sustained work across painting, landscape design, plant collecting and botany, sculpture, textile and jewellery design, stage sets, parks administration in Recife and university teaching. Breadth is well documented; depth in each field is not scored.

proactive_agency.rationale: [src_bm_icomos, src_bm_tclf, src_bm_britannica | 1930-1985 | expert evaluation, foundation profile, reference biography] Self-started projects are documented: converting his home into a tropical plant centre after 1930, buying the Sitio land in 1949 and adding parcels in 1952 and 1960 for the collection, formalising his office as Burle Marx & Cia. in 1955, and donating the property in 1985. The Sitio episodes rest mainly on ICOMOS and the Brazilian dossier; lowered slightly during calibration.

impact_motivation.rationale: [src_bm_icomos, src_bm_britannica, src_bm_tclf, src_bm_boifava, src_bm_eliovson | 1960s-1985 | expert evaluation, reference biography, foundation profile, scholarly article, garden-writer profile] He donated the Sitio to the federal government in 1985 and stayed as its first director; sources record his public appeals against deforestation (Britannica, TCLF, Eliovson) and a 1983 conference arguing for educational parks and gardens (Boifava). The advocacy statements are mostly his own words restated by sympathetic sources; lowered during calibration.

collaboration.rationale: [src_bm_adams, src_bm_mam, src_bm_boifava, src_bm_eliovson | 1950s-1990 | exhibition-catalogue biography, museum record, scholarly article, garden-writer profile] Adams describes an office where everyone joins the first discussions and he listens to all suggestions, working closely with his partner Haruyoshi Ono; MAM Rio and Boifava record associated architects, the botanists Mello Barreto and Mello Filho, and the Flamengo Park working group under Lota de Macedo Soares; Eliovson names the two chief architects who worked with him. Several independent accounts describe teamwork; credit-sharing at Flamengo is documented, not claimed for him alone.

conflict_tolerance.rationale: [src_bm_adams | 1956-1961 | exhibition-catalogue biography] Adams, citing a 1963 magazine account, says he declined an early invitation to work on Brasilia because Kubitschek, as mayor of Belo Horizonte, had not paid for earlier work, and describes the unfinished Caracas park as showing visions that respect neither politicians nor budgets. One second-hand episode and one authorial characterisation; lowered during calibration.

portrait.source: Photograph of Roberto Burle Marx dated December 1961, Arquivo Nacional (Brazilian National Archives), Fundo Agencia Nacional, reference BR_RJANRIO_EH_0_FOT_PPU_4919_d008, published by the Arquivo Nacional on its official Flickr account (uploaded 24 October 2017) with the Public Domain Mark; the same file is on Wikimedia Commons as 'Burle Marx.jpg'. The Flickr original (3560 x 3976 pixels) was cropped to remove the institution's corner logo and a bystander at the left edge and downscaled to 915 x 1000 with no upscaling. The photographer is not named.

provenance.notes: portrait_preflight: PLAUSIBLE (Stage B) / lead did NOT survive: the Marcio Scavone studio portrait (CC BY-SA 4.0, 1992) rests on uploader self-attestation with no corroboration of authorship or date, and the aroid Flickr 1981 image has an unreadable source page; the 1955 Arquivo Nacional Correio da Manha item carries restrictive holder terms. REPLACEMENT: Arquivo Nacional, Fundo Agencia Nacional, December 1961 (found by checking the Commons category), published by the holder on its official Flickr with the Public Domain Mark; the Flickr item page was read (title 'Burle Marx', description, date, reference code, Public Domain Mark). Sitter: holder title plus visual match to the 1955 Correio da Manha photograph (a different Arquivo Nacional fonds). Caveats: the rights basis is the holder's declaration, not age (photographer unnamed, Brazilian photograph term not expired); the Arquivo Nacional FAQ separately says reproductions it supplies require a signed responsibility term and fee, which concerns its reproduction service, not this public release; the SIAN catalogue record was not opened. QID VERIFIED LIVE 2026-11-24 (Q528922, human, 1909-1994). REGION latin_america. ZERO POLITICS. Korean name is a transliteration (no Korean source found).
